# Admission config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/admission/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.AdmissionBlock` — the per-principal governance ceilings ADR-075 D9 calls configuration rather than architecture. A singleton kind: at most one `admission` block across the vault.

The block is nested per resource owner, because a dimension is registered by the consumer that owns the resource (ADR-075 D3): `mcp` and `feeds` bound their own adapters (an `a2a` block is refused at load by name, ADR-136 D8 having dropped the adapter it bounded — delete it); `volumes`, `environments`, `shells`, `desktops` and `ptys` bound a principal across every protocol it arrives on; `guidance` bounds what one caller may push into somebody else's running work; `signin` bounds what the issuer's sign-in doors may send and how many people one person may invite (ADR-170 D11); `email` bounds how many messages each of the email service's two senders may hand to the provider in an hour (ADR-169 D12); and `dispatch` sizes the capability lane pool every adapter shares. There is deliberately no adapter-blind "everything" ceiling — one number spanning two protocols would be a ceiling nobody owns.

An omitted attribute takes the `deployment_profile` default; every ceiling is a pointer so that `0` (refuse everything) and `-1` (unlimited) stay expressible and distinct from "unset". `signin` departs from both halves of that, deliberately: its defaults are one table for every profile (1 and 5 codes a minute and an hour, 50 pending invitations and 20 a day per inviter), and its two code-send rates refuse `0` and `-1` — turning the code door off is `auth { issuer { email_code { enabled } } }`'s decision, and an unbounded sender at addresses strangers type is not a posture. Its invitation limits keep the sentinels. `email`'s two rates default to 10 an hour each under `server` and `embedded` and to unlimited under `dev`, keep `-1` for unlimited, and refuse `0` — turning a sender's mail off is the `email` kind's presence; without an `email` kind the block bounds nothing, and `tera config plan` warns that it does.

Relocated out of the bootstrap-HCL kernel by ADR-122 D5, and the kernel spelling is retired rather than retained as an escape hatch. An edit here takes effect on the NEXT admission decision for the dimension it names: the shared governor's policy for that dimension is replaced in place, keeping every principal's accumulated usage, its window end and its live leases. A principal already holding more than a newly lowered ceiling keeps what it holds and is refused its next acquisition — nothing in flight is evicted or re-admitted (ADR-122 D6). A changed meter window is used when the next window opens rather than retiming one already running. Withdrawing the block returns every ceiling to its profile default rather than freezing the last authored value.

`deployment_profile` did NOT move with it and is not authorable here: these ceilings resolve against that profile, and ADR-122 D2 keeps it kernel-only as trust posture — a vault edit that could change it would let the thing being governed widen its own governance.

A reload whose result would violate ADR-075 D4's isolation invariant — a per-principal in-flight cap at or above the number of lanes serving a capability, under the server profile — is refused before it commits, with nothing applied (ADR-122 D3).

One bound on that refusal is worth knowing before scaling both numbers up together: `dispatch.lanes` reaches capabilities served from NOW ON, while the ceilings reach the next decision immediately, so a capability already being served keeps the pool it started with. Raising the in-flight cap above the pool those capabilities already have passes the check and leaves them without the isolation property until each is re-registered or the daemon restarts. Lowering a cap, or raising lanes without raising the cap, cannot produce that.

## Example

A minimal `admission`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/admission/example-admission.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

admission {}
```

## `mcp` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `inflight` | integer | no | — | — | — | Per-principal ceiling on concurrently in-flight MCP gateway requests. Omitted resolves to the deployment profile's default; -1 is unlimited; 0 refuses every request. Values below -1 are refused at validate. |
| `shell_idle_ttl` | string | no | — | — | — | How long an idle MCP-exposed shell, and the MCP session that may hold one, survives before the reaper reclaims it, as a Go duration ("8h", "30m"). Omitted resolves to the profile default: 8h in the server and gateway profiles, 24h elsewhere. A negative duration disables reaping, so a shell lives until it is released or the daemon restarts; zero is refused. A shell with a call in flight is never idle. session_idle_ttl is its equal legacy alias: writing either is complete, and writing both with different values is refused (ADR-076 Amendment 2). Hot-reloaded. |
| `shell_sweep_interval` | string | no | `5m` | — | — | How often the reaper looks for idle shells and sessions, as a Go duration. An abandoned shell is reclaimed within shell_idle_ttl plus this interval, not at the TTL. A non-positive value disables the reaper outright, anonymous sessions included. session_sweep_interval is its equal legacy alias, on the same terms as shell_idle_ttl's. |
| `shell_output_cap` | string | no | `8KiB` | — | — | The most bytes one stream, stdout or stderr, of an MCP-exposed bash result may carry, as a byte size ("8KiB", "16KB"). A stream over it is never returned in part: all of it is written to a file in the shell, named by $SPILL (or $SPILL_ERR), and the result says where it is, how big it is and, for JSON, its shape. It bounds only what a call returns; data flowing between commands inside the shell is never capped. The default is well inside the most restrictive common client: Codex CLI keeps only the first and last parts of a result over about 10,000 tokens and marks the cut (measured 2026-10-08), and two streams at 8KiB are about 4,000 tokens. At most 64MiB. Hot-reloaded (ADR-076 Amendment 7). |
| `shell_output_ceiling` | string | no | `32MiB` | — | — | The most bytes one stream may carry on a call that passes full_output: true, which otherwise lifts shell_output_cap for that call. It protects the daemon and the gateway, which hold a result in memory whole; above it the stream is spilled exactly as it is over the cap, and the result says the ceiling was hit. At most 64MiB, because the channel between the daemon and the shell's helper process is sized from it; a ceiling below the cap is raised to the cap. Hot-reloaded. |
| `session_idle_ttl` | string | no | — | — | — | Legacy-era spelling of shell_idle_ttl, kept first-class through the dual-era window: identical meaning, resolution and reaper. Prefer shell_idle_ttl; validate warns on a lone session_idle_ttl and refuses the two set to different values (ADR-076 Amendment 2 A2.5). |
| `session_sweep_interval` | string | no | `5m` | — | — | Legacy-era spelling of shell_sweep_interval, on the same terms as session_idle_ttl. Prefer shell_sweep_interval. |
| `calls_per_interval` | integer | no | — | — | — | Per-principal ceiling on MCP client requests per meter_interval. One tools/call is one call, and one aggregate tools/list is one call however many upstreams it sweeps (ADR-075 D6). Omitted resolves to the profile default; -1 is unlimited; 0 refuses every request. |
| `bytes` | integer | no | — | — | — | Per-principal ceiling on request-body bytes per meter_interval: inbound only, the bytes the caller pushed at the gateway, not responses and not far-side forwards. Omitted resolves to the profile default; -1 is unlimited; 0 refuses every request. |
| `meter_interval` | string | no | `1m` | — | — | The window both cumulative meters, calls_per_interval and bytes, roll on, as a Go duration ("1m", "30s"). One window for both, and not profile-keyed, because it is the unit both ceilings are quoted in. It is a hard edge rather than a sliding average: the counters reset when it rolls, so a principal that spends its budget in the first second waits out the remainder. |

## `email` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `issuer_per_hour` | integer | no | — | — | — | How many messages the issuer — sign-in codes, invitations and passkey notices — may hand to the provider in an hour, across every recipient. Omitted takes the profile default: 10 an hour under server and embedded, unlimited under dev. -1 is unlimited; 0 is refused, because turning the issuer's mail off is the email kind's presence and auth.issuer.email_code.enabled. A send past it is refused rather than queued; the per-address sign-in limits are admission.signin's and are counted before this. |
| `correspondence_per_hour` | integer | no | — | — | — | How many messages the correspondence carrier may hand to the provider in an hour, across every window. Omitted takes the profile default: 10 an hour under server and embedded, unlimited under dev. -1 is unlimited; 0 is refused, because turning correspondence mail off is the email kind's presence. A refused send is recorded as a delivery failure and the message continues to the recipient's other windows. |
